questions.stem: Mr Peralta, 41, has known rheumatoid arthritis and is on the rheumatology ward. On inspecting his hands you see ulnar deviation at the MCPs and swan neck deformities. The examiner asks how you would tell at the bedside whether these are rheumatoid deformities or the Jaccoud's arthropathy of SLE. Which examination step best answers this?
options: Perform Tinel's test by tapping over the carpal tunnel at the wrist crease
Squeeze gently across the MCP joints and watch his face for pain
Gently try to correct each deformity passively and see if it reduces
Ask him to make a fist and watch whether the fingers flex fully
questions.why: Jaccoud's deformities in SLE come from lax capsules and ligaments without erosion, so they correct passively. Rheumatoid deformities come from erosion and joint destruction and are usually fixed. Gentle passive correction tells them apart.
notes: Tinel's test looks for median nerve compression (carpal tunnel syndrome is common in RA) and tells you nothing about whether a deformity is fixed or reversible.
A positive MCP squeeze shows active synovitis, which occurs in both conditions, so it does not tell you whether the deformity is fixed.
Making a fist assesses function and range of movement, but it does not test whether a deformity can be passively corrected.

questions.stem: Mr Peralta, 41, is on the rheumatology ward with a flare of rheumatoid arthritis after 5 months off methotrexate. He has never had a biological medicine, his liver and kidney function are normal, and he does not know whether he has ever been tested for hepatitis. Which test should be done before methotrexate is restarted?
options: Baseline retinal examination by an ophthalmologist
Repeat anti-CCP titre to guide the starting dose
questions.why: Methotrexate is toxic to the liver and suppresses the immune system, so hepatitis B and C serology is done before starting or restarting it (with FBC, LFT, UEC and a baseline chest X-ray). This protects against hepatitis B reactivation and added liver injury.
notes: TPMT activity is checked before starting azathioprine, not methotrexate.
A baseline eye examination is for hydroxychloroquine, because of retinal toxicity, not methotrexate.
Anti-CCP confirms the diagnosis and predicts erosive disease, but it isn't used to monitor disease or set methotrexate doses.

questions.stem: Mr Peralta, 41, has a flare of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis. His bloods show Hb 118 g/L, MCV 86 fL, platelets 452 x 10^9/L and CRP 46 mg/L. He stopped methotrexate 5 months ago and has taken ibuprofen for 3 weeks. Which mechanism most likely explains his anaemia?
options: Folate deficiency from methotrexate slowing DNA synthesis in red cell precursors
Blood loss in the gut from ibuprofen draining his iron stores
Anti-CCP antibodies binding red cells and causing haemolysis by complement
IL-6 raises hepcidin, which blocks ferroportin and traps iron in macrophages
questions.why: In anaemia of chronic disease, inflammatory cytokines (mainly IL-6) make the liver produce hepcidin. Hepcidin breaks down ferroportin, so the gut absorbs less iron and iron stays locked in macrophages. The result is a normocytic anaemia, often with a high platelet count, and a normal or high ferritin.
notes: Folate deficiency would cause a macrocytic anaemia, and he stopped methotrexate 5 months ago.
Three weeks of ibuprofen is unlikely to empty iron stores, and iron deficiency would usually give a low MCV. It's still worth checking iron studies.
Anti-CCP antibodies target citrullinated proteins in the joints, not red cells, and RA doesn't usually cause haemolysis.

questions.stem: Mr Peralta, 41, has had erosive rheumatoid arthritis since he was 29 and says his neck is a bit stiff in the mornings. Long-standing RA puts him at risk of atlantoaxial subluxation, which matters for neck manipulation and intubation. Erosion and laxity of which structure mainly allows this subluxation?
options: Ligamentum flavum joining the laminae of C1 and C2
Transverse ligament of the atlas behind the dens
Anterior longitudinal ligament at the C1 to C2 level
Nuchal ligament attached to the spinous process of C2
questions.why: The transverse ligament of the atlas holds the dens against the back of the anterior arch of C1. Rheumatoid synovitis erodes and weakens it, so the dens can move backwards and compress the cervical cord, especially when the neck is flexed.
notes: The ligamentum flavum joins the laminae behind the spinal canal and doesn't hold the dens in place.
The anterior longitudinal ligament runs down the front of the vertebral bodies and doesn't stop the dens moving backwards.
The nuchal ligament is a superficial midline ligament of the back of the neck and plays no part in atlantoaxial stability.
